summary: Defines the /.well-known/ path prefix for well-known locations in selected URI schemes. It obsoletes RFC 5785, updates the URI schemes in RFC 7230 to reserve that space, and updates RFC 7595. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Some web applications need to check something about a site before they act on it, for example whether they may crawl the pages or what privacy policy applies. This RFC reserves one path, /.well-known/, for such site-wide files, so every application can find its own file there and no two applications use the same name.

questions: how to register a well-known uri
subtitle: A reserved /.well-known/ path so a protocol can find site-wide files without colliding with a site's own pages.

tldr.problem: Applications often need information about a site before they can talk to it, such as permission to crawl it or its privacy policy, and there was no agreed place to put such information.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reserves the path prefix /.well-known/ in the HTTP, HTTPS, WebSocket and Secure WebSocket schemes, and sets up a registry where each application registers the name it will use there.
tldr.outcome: The RFC replaced RFC 5785, allowed well-known URIs in non-Web schemes, and started tracking which URI schemes support them.

today: RFC 8615 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 5785, updated the URI schemes in RFC 7230 to reserve the path, and updated RFC 7595 to track which schemes support well-known URIs.

sections.title: Why Well-Known Locations Are Needed
sections.content:
Some web applications need to discover information about an origin, sometimes called site-wide metadata, before they make a request. The Robots Exclusion Protocol, at robotstxt.org, is one example: it gives automated processes a way to obtain permission to access resources. The Platform for Privacy Preferences tells user agents how to discover a privacy policy before they interact with an origin server.

There are other ways to reach per-resource metadata, such as HTTP header fields or the PROPFIND method of WebDAV, but the overhead of those approaches, in client-perceived latency or in deployment difficulty, often rules them out for this purpose.

At the same time, HTTP has become a common substrate for protocols that are not part of the web, and those protocols sometimes need to find one or more resources on a given host. The obvious answer is to designate a well-known location for data or services belonging to the site as a whole, so that it is easy to find. The drawback is that this risks collisions, both with other well-known locations and with resources the site has already created or wants to create, and it takes some of the site's control over its own URI space away from it.
sections.plainLanguage: A program often needs something from a website before it can do its job, such as a file saying which pages may be crawled. Putting that file at a path everyone agrees on is simple, but two programs could end up wanting the same path, and the site owner may already use it for something else.

sections.title: The Reserved Path Prefix
sections.content:
A well-known URI is a URI whose path component begins with the characters /.well-known/, provided that the scheme is explicitly defined to support well-known URIs. If an application registers the name 'example', the corresponding well-known URI on http://www.example.com/ is http://www.example.com/.well-known/example.

This specification updates the http and https schemes of RFC 7230 to support well-known URIs. Other schemes can be given the same treatment by updating their own definitions, as RFC 8307 does for the ws and wss schemes. Well-known URIs may also be used with other schemes, but only where the definition of the scheme explicitly allows it. The registry of URI schemes now tracks which schemes support well-known URIs.

Several limits apply. Registered names must conform to the segment-nz production of RFC 3986, so they cannot contain the slash character, and they should be precise for the application rather than a generic term: for metadata the Example application might register 'example-metadata' or 'example.com-metadata', not 'metadata'.

Well-known URIs are rooted at the top of the path hierarchy. /.well-known/example is a well-known URI, while /foo/.well-known/example is not. The RFC does not define a format or media type for the resource at /.well-known/ itself, and clients should not expect one to exist there. It also does not define how to work out the host name to use, nor the scope of the metadata that is found; both are for the application to decide.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is short: the path has to start with /.well-known/ and the scheme has to allow it. Everything after the prefix is a name the application registers, so that two applications cannot pick the same one.

sections.title: Registering a Well-Known URI
sections.content:
An application that wants to mint a new well-known URI must register it in the Well-Known URI registry. A registration request carries at least the URI suffix, the name requested relative to /.well-known/; the change controller, which is 'IETF' for a Standards Track RFC and the name of the responsible party otherwise; the specification document that defines the field, preferably with a URI from which it can be retrieved; and a status of either 'permanent' or 'provisional'. It may also carry related information, and registrations may include the syntax of extra path components, query strings or fragment identifiers, or protocol-specific details such as HTTP method handling.

The specification has to say which URI schemes the well-known URI may be used with. If no schemes are named, http and https are assumed. Applications will normally use the default port for the scheme, and any alternative port has to be stated by the application.

Values defined by Standards Track RFCs and other open standards have the status 'permanent'. Other values can also be registered as permanent if the experts find them in use, and other values should be registered as 'provisional'. The experts may remove a provisional entry if they find it is not in use, and may change a provisional entry to permanent after considering how widely used the value is and consulting the community. A third party, including the experts themselves, may register a well-known URI if the experts decide an unregistered one is widely deployed and unlikely to be registered in time, but such a registration still has to meet the requirements, including referencing a specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using a name, an application puts it into a public registry and points at the document that defines what will be found there. The registry marks each entry as permanent or provisional, so that unused names can be handed back later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists the issues that applications minting well-known URIs and the administrators deploying them have to consider: exposure of sensitive data, denial-of-service attacks in addition to normal load issues, server and client authentication, vulnerability to DNS rebinding attacks, and attacks in which limited access to a server grants the ability to affect how well-known URIs are served.

Because a well-known location effectively represents the entire origin, server operators should control the ability to write to it. That matters most when more than one entity shares an origin, but even a single-entity origin should make sure that write access to well-known locations is not granted unwittingly, whether through server configuration or through implementation permissions on a filesystem.

Well-known resources on http and https URLs are reachable by web browsers, so they can be manipulated by content from other parts of the same origin: an attacker who can inject content, for example through a cross-site scripting flaw, can make potentially arbitrary requests to the well-known resource. HTTP and HTTPS also use origins as a security boundary for cookies, web storage and other capabilities, so an application that defines a well-known location should not assume it has sole access to them or that it is the only application on the origin. The mitigations the RFC lists include encrypting sensitive information, using an application-specific media type and failing if it is not used, using the HttpOnly and Path cookie flags, sending X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, using Content-Security-Policy, using Referrer-Policy, and avoiding compression on sensitive information, since an attacker with access to the communication path can use compression to recover it.

The RFC also warns about scope. This memo does not specify the scope of applicability of the information found at a well-known URI, nor how to discover one, so each application must define both. Letting https://example.com/.well-known/example set policy for https://department.example.com or https://www.example.com:8000 assumes a relationship between hosts where there may be none, and gives control to a potential attacker. Using a well-known URI to bootstrap a separate service, such as email policy, can produce a flood of requests to web servers that do not implement it, which can look like a denial-of-service attack.

Finally, some server administrators may be unaware that a well-known location exists, especially on operating systems that hide directories whose names begin with a dot. An attacker with write access to the .well-known directory could therefore control its contents without the administrator realising it.
sections.plainLanguage: A file that stands for the whole site needs the same care as the site itself. Anyone who can write it can change what every client of that site does, and a site that does not notice that its .well-known directory is being written to has no warning.

sections.title: Registry Assignments
sections.content:
Well-known URIs are registered on the advice of one or more experts, with a Specification Required, using the terminology of RFC 8126. The experts' primary considerations are conformance to the requirements of Section 3, the availability and stability of the specifying document, and the security considerations in Section 4. IANA directs senders of registry requests to this document and to any process the experts have established.

IANA has updated the registration procedure to Specification Required, added a Status column to the registry, and marked all existing registrations as permanent.

The registry of URI schemes gains a field named 'Well-Known URI Support', whose default value is a dash. When a scheme has been specified to use well-known URIs, the value becomes a reference to that specification. The initial values that are not a dash are coap and coaps, pointing to RFC 7252; coap+tcp, coap+ws, coaps+tcp and coaps+ws, pointing to RFC 8323; http and https, pointing to this RFC; and ws and wss, pointing to RFC 8307.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC also updates two public lists. One records which names have been registered, with a note of whether each one is permanent. The other records which kinds of address, such as http or coap, are allowed to use the reserved path at all.

sections.title: What Changed From RFC 5785
sections.content:
This document replaces RFC 5785. The changes it lists are: well-known locations that are not part of the web are now allowed, the IANA instructions were adjusted, references were updated, various clarifications were made, and the schemes that support well-known URIs are now tracked in the URI schemes registry.

The frequently asked questions in Appendix A explain the reasoning. Well-known locations do have drawbacks, for both technical and social reasons, but they are sometimes necessary, and this memo defines a sandbox for them to reduce the risk of collision and to limit the effect on URIs that already exist on a site. The prefix /.well-known/ was chosen because it is short and descriptive and, according to search indices, not widely used. Existing mechanisms such as P3P and robots.txt are unaffected until they choose to use this one. Per-directory well-known locations, such as /images/.well-known/, were not defined, because they would raise the risk of colliding with URIs a site already has, and because such solutions do not scale well since they are too chatty.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier version of this idea, RFC 5785, applied only to the web. This one also allows other kinds of address to use the reserved path, and it records which schemes have opted in. The rest of the rules, including the choice of the name .well-known, stayed the same.

items.title: URI suffix
items.text: The name relative to /.well-known/, such as example. No slash allowed.

items.title: Change controller
items.text: IETF for a Standards Track RFC, otherwise the responsible party.

items.title: Specification
items.text: The document that defines the field and its media types.

items.title: Schemes
items.text: Which URI schemes it may be used with; http and https are assumed.
